reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO & national toxicology guidance
clinicalPearls: Toxicity relates to the amount of elemental iron ingested, not the total salt weight, so the specific preparation must be identified

The classic course has recognised stages: early GI toxicity, a deceptive latent phase of apparent improvement, then shock and metabolic acidosis, hepatic failure, and finally late gastric scarring and outlet obstruction
Early severe vomiting, diarrhoea, and haematemesis reflect direct corrosive injury to the gut mucosa
Do not be misled by the quiescent second phase; serious systemic toxicity can still evolve after the patient seems to settle
Radiopaque tablets may be visible on an abdominal radiograph and can confirm ingestion and guide decontamination
Whole-bowel irrigation is the preferred decontamination method for significant ingestions, as activated charcoal does not bind iron
Deferoxamine is the specific chelating antidote, indicated for systemic toxicity, shock, significant acidosis, or high serum iron levels
A high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, hypotension, and progressive hepatic injury mark severe poisoning requiring urgent chelation and intensive support
reference.pathophysiology: In overdose, free iron overwhelms the body's binding capacity (transferrin) and circulates unbound. It is directly corrosive to the gastrointestinal mucosa, causing haemorrhagic gastroenteritis and fluid loss. Absorbed free iron is a potent catalyst of free-radical formation and disrupts mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, causing cellular injury most prominently in the liver, along with a high anion-gap metabolic (lactic) acidosis. Iron-induced vasodilatation, increased capillary permeability, and myocardial depression produce shock. Healing of the corrosive gastric injury can later cause strictures and gastric outlet obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of high anion-gap metabolic acidosis
additionalInvestigations: Serum iron level, ideally timed to peak absorption
Arterial blood gas with anion gap and lactate
Liver function tests and coagulation profile to track hepatic injury
Full blood count, electrolytes, renal function, and glucose
redFlags: Haematemesis or melaena indicating corrosive GI injury
Hypotension, shock, or lethargy signalling systemic toxicity
High anion-gap metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate
Evidence of hepatic injury or coagulopathy
Persistent or worsening symptoms after the apparent latent phase
reference.prognosis: Small ingestions causing only GI upset usually resolve, but severe poisoning with shock, acidosis, and hepatic failure carries significant mortality; early recognition, decontamination, and deferoxamine chelation greatly improve survival, though late gastric strictures may still occur.
pitfalls: Calculating dose from tablet weight rather than elemental iron content
Discharging a patient during the deceptive latent phase before systemic toxicity manifests
Giving activated charcoal, which does not adsorb iron
Delaying deferoxamine in a patient with shock, acidosis, or high iron levels
management: Resuscitate aggressively with intravenous fluids to counter corrosive gastrointestinal losses and iron-induced vasodilatory shock
Decontaminate the gut with whole-bowel irrigation for significant ingestions, since activated charcoal does not bind iron, confirming clearance with abdominal radiography
Chelate with intravenous deferoxamine in severe poisoning marked by shock, metabolic acidosis, high serum iron or significant symptoms
Correct the metabolic acidosis and support evolving hepatic failure and coagulopathy
Monitor closely through the deceptive latent phase, as systemic toxicity can progress after apparent improvement
Anticipate and manage late gastric outlet obstruction from strictures with endoscopy or surgery
Involve the poisons information service and, in children, assess safeguarding and future prevention
